title: Matching Higher-Degree Power Functions y = x^4, y = x^7, y = x^10 to Their Graphs
originalTopic: Theory and Examples: Power Function Comparison
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Match each equation (a) y = x^4, (b) y = x^7, and (c) y = x^10 with its corresponding curve (f, g, or h), where curve f lies in Quadrants I and III, and curves g and h lie in Quadrants I and II with curve g flatter near 0 and steeper for |x| > 1 than curve h. Justify your reasoning without a graphing device.
finalAnswer: \text{(a) } y = x^4 \to h; \quad \text{(b) } y = x^7 \to f; \quad \text{(c) } y = x^{10} \to g

steps.title: Identify the Odd Power Function by Quadrant Symmetry
steps.mathExpression: y = x^7 \text{ is odd } \implies \text{Graph } f \text{ (Quadrants I and III)}
steps.explanation: Among x^4, x^7, and x^10, only y = x^7 has an odd exponent, so it takes negative values for x < 0 and is symmetric about the origin. Therefore, (b) y = x^7 matches curve f.
steps.why: Odd powers preserve the sign of x, placing their graphs in Quadrants I and III.

steps.title: Compare the Even Power Functions y = x^4 and y = x^10
steps.explanation: Both y = x^4 and y = x^10 are even functions symmetric about the y-axis, intersecting at (-1, 1), (0, 0), and (1, 1). On (-1, 1), raising a fraction to the 10th power makes it smaller than the 4th power, so y = x^10 lies below y = x^4; for |x| > 1, y = x^10 grows much faster and lies above y = x^4.
steps.why: Higher even exponents flatten the graph closer to 0 on (-1, 1) and steepen the graph on |x| > 1.

steps.title: State the Complete Matching
steps.mathExpression: \text{(a) } y = x^4 \leftrightarrow h, \quad \text{(b) } y = x^7 \leftrightarrow f, \quad \text{(c) } y = x^{10} \leftrightarrow g
steps.explanation: Curve h (higher on (-1, 1) and lower for |x| > 1) is (a) y = x^4, curve f is (b) y = x^7, and curve g (flatter on (-1, 1) and steeper for |x| > 1) is (c) y = x^10.
steps.why: Symmetry separates the odd power from the even powers, and relative magnitude on (0, 1) vs (1, inf) separates x^4 from x^10.
